column6: Moses' hands become heavy, and Aaron and Hur hold them up from opposite sides; this is the commentary's concrete image of a failing body steadied by people on both sides.
The wilderness wanderers cry to the LORD in distress and are delivered; it supplies a narrative form for the move from a stranded traveler to nasta'inu, asking for aid.
After their cry, God leads the wanderers by a straight way to a settled place; it closely joins requested help to ihdina and the straight route.

column5: q-w-m B002; arise and hold a hand
column6: Genesis tells Hagar to arise (Hebrew qumi) and to hold the boy's hand in the wilderness; the genuine q-w-m cognate joins the source's uprightness to hand-held aid.
The angel tells exhausted Elijah to arise and eat because the journey is too much for him; Hebrew qum gives the source's q-w-m standing image a traveler-specific setting of divine provision.
Strengthened by the food, Elijah travels forty days to Horeb; this realizes the commentary's sequence in which help restores a body for the road.
God gives power to the faint and strength to the powerless, directly matching the source's weak traveler who cannot proceed unaided.
Those who wait for the LORD receive renewed strength and walk without fainting; it gives the commentary's aided and composed walking an explicit divine outcome.
The speaker's words uphold one who stumbles and make weak knees firm; this supplies a verbal and social analogue to the bodily support in the commentary.
Job says he was feet to the lame; the figure makes another person capable of movement, as the source's helpers make a weak walker mobile.

column5: holding the right hand; divine help
column6: God takes Israel's right hand and says, I help you; it fuses the commentary's hand-supported traveler with its explicit request for help.
God promises to strengthen, help, and uphold with the righteous right hand; the three actions closely mirror aid becoming upright stability.
The LORD supports all who fall and raises those bowed down; it gives a divine counterpart to the source's movement from collapse toward an upright body.
Though the righteous fall, they are not cast down because the LORD holds their hand; the text makes support at the moment of failed footing the reason for recovery.
Angels bear the faithful person on their hands lest a foot strike a stone; it is a particularly close scriptural image for support that protects a traveler's gait.
The pilgrim identifies the LORD as the source of help; beside nasta'inu it makes aid a prayerful reliance rather than merely an abstract resource.
The helper will not let the pilgrim's foot slip; it makes the aid of the preceding verse legible in the commentary's terms of stable walking.
God's everlasting arms are beneath Israel; this gives the source's image of being borne from the sides a protective, sustaining underside.
The prophetic command to strengthen weak hands and make feeble knees firm directly shares the commentary's debilitated body before it can walk well.

column5: highway; walkers do not go astray
column6: The Way of Holiness is a highway on which even inexperienced walkers do not go astray; it brings bodily frailty and a protected route into one prophetic scene.

column5: this is the way; right or left
column6: A voice tells the traveler, This is the way, walk in it, when turning right or left; it answers the commentary's swaying walker with directional guidance.
God leads the returning people by watercourses on a straight path where they will not stumble; this is an unusually close pairing of divine leading, straightness, and safe feet.

column5: leading the blind; rough ground level
column6: God leads blind people on an unknown way and makes rough places level; it extends the source's guide beyond a front-runner to aid for those unable to navigate alone.
The LORD continually guides, satisfies need in parched places, and makes the bones strong; this joins the commentary's need, support, and restored movement.
Acknowledging God results in paths made straight; it is a concise wisdom analogue to the communal petition for the straight path.
The teacher leads the pupil in the way of wisdom and paths of uprightness; it joins route-guidance to the moral and bodily verticality heard in mustaqim.

column5: unhampered steps; no stumble in running
column6: The instructed walker has unhampered steps and does not stumble even when running; it gives a contrast to the source's impaired gait and its recovery.

column5: do not turn right or left
column6: The command not to swerve right or left and to keep the foot from evil makes the commentary's literal side-to-side wavering an ethical path image.
The proverb says that one who hastens with the feet misses the way; it supplies a wisdom contrast to the source's calm, non-panicked good walking.
The LORD goes before Israel in a pillar to lead the way; it brings together the commentary's guide, road, and qiyam-as-pillar imagery.
The shepherd seeks the lost, binds the injured, and strengthens the weak; it converts the source's individual supporting act into pastoral responsibility.
The source labels na'budu with the 'ayn-b-d root; Isaiah calls the chosen eved God's servant and says God upholds him, a cognate service-and-support pairing.
The source labels malik with m-l-k; Isaiah's melek is the cognate king term and names the LORD as king who saves us, tying sovereignty to needed deliverance.

column5: help the weak against the mighty
column6: Asa asks God to help the powerless against the mighty because none is like God in helping; this makes the source's request for aid an explicit prayer from weakness.

column5: servants' eyes toward a master's hand
column6: The psalm likens its dependence on the LORD's mercy to servants watching their master's hand; it gives the juxtaposition of na'budu and nasta'inu a relational image.
When one person falls, the other lifts the companion; it supplies the social logic behind the source's weak traveler being held rather than left alone.

column5: traveler seeks someone who knows the road
column6: Raphael says he knows the roads to Media and has traveled them often; Tobias's journey turns the request for guidance into finding a competent companion.
Wisdom guides the fleeing righteous person on straight paths; this is a Jewish-scriptural personification of the guidance sought in ihdina.

column5: level ground so Israel walks safely
column6: God levels mountains and fills valleys so Israel may walk safely; it develops the source's straightened route as a bodily safe passage.

column5: traveler's prayer for leading and safe arrival
column6: The Tefillat ha-Derekh asks God to lead, guide, sustain, and bring the traveler to the destination in peace; it is a direct Jewish liturgical analogue to asking aid and a way.

column5: rider on a donkey directs the heart
column6: The mishnah treats a rider on a donkey who cannot dismount for prayer and directs the heart toward the sanctuary; it keeps the source's mount-bound traveler inside a disciplined prayer practice.
The exhortation to lift drooping hands and strengthen weak knees takes up the same weakened limbs that the commentary imagines before aid.

column5: straight paths for feet; lame healed
column6: Straight paths are to be made for the feet so that the lame may be healed rather than dislocated; it is one of the closest Christian fusions of straight path, gait, and restoration.
Peter takes the lame man by the right hand and raises him, and his feet and ankles become strong; it gives the source's hand-held help a concrete upright result.
The healed man leaps up, stands, and walks; this provides the full bodily sequence that the commentary reads into aid followed by upright movement.
The woman's disabling spirit leaves her bent and unable to straighten; it supplies an exact counter-image to the upright mustaqim walker.
After Jesus lays hands on her, the woman is immediately made straight; the touch makes aid visibly become upright posture.

column5: no one to help the disabled man
column6: The disabled man says he has no person to put him into the pool; this sharpens the commentary's premise that a weak traveler cannot manage alone.
Jesus commands the man to rise, carry his bed, and walk; it gives the source's requested help its compact standing-and-road outcome.
Four people carry the paralytic to Jesus; the scene makes communal bodily assistance the condition of bringing an immobilized person forward.
The paralytic is told to rise, take up his mat, and go home; it turns the carried body's recovery into independent walking.
Paul commands a man disabled in his feet to stand upright, and he leaps and walks; its wording explicitly joins uprightness to restored motion.

column5: injured traveler placed on an animal
column6: The Samaritan binds an injured traveler's wounds, puts him on his own animal, and brings him to care; it reverses the source's failed mount into a means of carrying the weak.

column5: weary and burdened invited to rest
column6: Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come for rest; it gives the commentary's exhausted traveler a direct address and relief.

column5: gentle yoke and rest for souls
column6: Taking Jesus' gentle yoke brings rest; it supplies a Christian image of a burden that supports rather than overwhelms the weak walker.
Peter begins to sink while walking and cries, Lord, save me; the scene makes the commentary's helpless request arise at a literal failure of footing.
Jesus immediately reaches out and takes the sinking man's hand; it is a direct one-handed counterpart to the source's supported traveler.
The Spirit helps human weakness when people do not know how to pray; it applies requested divine aid to the very act of supplication.
Approaching the throne yields mercy and grace for timely help; it sets the source's plea for aid before a sovereign, as malik frames the petition.
The strong are obliged to bear the frailties of the weak; it states the communal duty implicit in the commentary's two supporting companions.
Bearing one another's burdens makes bodily support an ethic of communal walking rather than an isolated rescue.
The community is told to help the weak and be patient with all; it pairs the source's assistance with the unhurried disposition of good walking.
The elders are reminded that one must help the weak; this concise imperative provides a communal form of the source's avn, help.

column5: guide feet into the way of peace
column6: The dawn from on high guides feet into the way of peace; it closely matches ihdina as guidance enacted at the feet.
John's proclamation uses Isaiah's command to make the Lord's paths straight; it gives the straight-path language a preparatory and eschatological Christian setting.

column5: How can I unless someone guides me?
column6: The Ethiopian traveler asks how he can understand unless someone guides him and invites Philip into the chariot; it turns guidance into companioned instruction on a journey.
The prayer of faith saves the sick and the Lord raises the person up; it joins prayer for aid to physical recovery and rising.

column5: the Lord stood by and strengthened me
column6: The Lord stands by Paul and strengthens him in abandonment; it gives the commentary's needed support a personal divine companion.
Believers are rooted, built up, and established in faith; it brings together the commentary's tree-on-roots and stable-wall images.

column5: body held together by supporting joints
column6: The whole body is joined and held together through every supporting joint; it translates the commentary's body-support image into reciprocal communal cohesion.

column5: house does not fall because founded on rock
column6: The house withstands storm because it has a rock foundation; it gives the source's wall and structural support imagery an ethical architectural counterpart.

column5: kept from stumbling and made to stand
column6: God is able to keep believers from stumbling and make them stand; it compresses the source's protected gait and upright result into doxology.

column5: tree with many roots resists wind
column6: Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah compares deeds exceeding wisdom to a tree with many roots that storms cannot uproot; it interprets rootedness as the moral stability behind the source's standing tree.

column5: sons of righteousness walk in paths of light
column6: The Community Rule places the sons of righteousness under the Prince of Lights and says they walk in paths of light; it gives the requested right way an angelic and communal Second Temple framing.

column5: walking after God means acts of care
column6: The talmudic reading of walking after God turns the command into clothing, visiting, comforting, and burying the vulnerable; it makes walking with God inseparable from supporting the weak.
The tempter cites angelic foot-protection to urge Jesus to leap; beside the source's needy petition, it raises the distinct question of asking for aid versus demanding a proof of it.
Jesus answers the appeal to protection by forbidding the testing of God; it supplies the interpretive boundary for the preceding scene's use of divine support.

column5: Jesus identifies himself as the way
column6: Where the source has a community ask God to guide it on a straight path, John identifies Jesus himself as the way to the Father; the contrast is a substantive Christological recasting of path language.
The Spirit of truth guides disciples into all truth; it extends the source's request for a guide from physical route-finding to discernment.

column5: Jesus joins travelers on the road
column6: Jesus draws near and travels with the disoriented disciples to Emmaus; it makes guidance take the form of a companion sharing the road.

column5: Lamb shepherds and guides to waters
column6: The Lamb shepherds the afflicted and guides them to springs of life-giving water; it combines leadership, relief, and a destination for the needy traveler.
The church is called the pillar and foundation of truth; it gives the commentary's qiyam-as-pillar image an ecclesial structural use.
Christ's power is made perfect in weakness; it supplies a theological reading in which the source's weakness remains the place where enabling aid is displayed.

column5: apart from me you can do nothing
column6: Branches can bear fruit only by remaining in the vine, and apart from Christ disciples can do nothing; it gives the source's inability to proceed alone an organic image of dependence.

column5: the Way of Life and the Way of Death
column6: The Didache opens with the Way of Life and the Way of Death; it supplies an early Christian ethical development of the path metaphor, though its two-way scheme goes beyond this section's single petition.
